meta.title: Who really said "A Gold Mine Is a Hole in the Ground with a Liar at the Top"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Bill Nye and not Mark Twain. The mining joke ran unsigned in the Detroit Free Press in 1881; Nye was credited in 1904, eight years after he died.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Gold Mine Is a Hole in the Ground with a Liar at the Top'?
meta.ogDescription: Bill Nye was credited in 1904, eight years after his death. The joke was anonymous newspaper filler in 1881. The documented trail, source by source.

answer.label: Not Bill Nye — an anonymous newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: First in print 9 November 1881 · the author was never named
answer.sourceLine: The Black Hills Illustrated credited this line to Bill Nye in 1904, eight years after he died — and called it his “paraphrase” rather than his invention, naming no source. Quote Investigator traces the joke to unsigned filler in the Detroit Free Press of 9 November 1881, fifteen years before Nye’s death, and concludes the originator was anonymous. Mark Twain, the name most often attached today, has no better claim.

source.heading: The 1904 book that pinned it on Bill Nye

docMeta.dd: “Looking Backward 56 Years: Broad Thoughts in Condensed Form,” by Major A. J. Simmons, M. E.
1904 · edited by George P. Baldwin under the auspices of the Black Hills Mining Men’s Association
Posthumous credit — Nye died in February 1896, and the book names no source

source.excerpt: This system of financiering was worked to such a degree that Bill Nye’s paraphrase of an early-day “gold mine,” “a hole in the ground, the owner whereof is a d—d liar,” came to be the popular accepted definition — and even at this late enlightened period there are instances where Mr. Nye’s theory of mines would find ample verification.
trail: 1881 — The earliest instance Quote Investigator can locate ↗ is an unsigned squib in the Detroit Free Press of 9 November 1881: “A mine is a hole in the ground. The discoverer of it is a natural liar.” No author, no speaker — newspaper filler, reprinted from New Haven to Chicago within a month.

1892–1903 — The joke starts collecting owners. A Mr. Walkup of Evanston, Illinois gets it in 1892; Mark Twain is first credited by a Marshall, Michigan paper in March 1896; the humorist Eli Perkins is credited at the American Mining Congress in September 1903 — all three traced by Quote Investigator ↗.

1904 — Bill Nye’s turn. The Black Hills Illustrated calls the line “Bill Nye’s paraphrase”; the sentence is readable in the Internet Archive’s scanned full text ↗. Nye had been dead eight years, and the book cites nothing.

1907 and after — The World’s Work prints the “liar at the top” shape in January 1907 and files it as an anonymous old adage, per Quote Investigator ↗. The Twain version only hardened in 1935, in The Autobiography of John Hays Hammond, p. 97 — where, twainquotes.com records ↗, there is “no other authentic record that Mark Twain made this statement.”
source.excerptNote: Read in the Internet Archive’s scan of the book. Note the word the author actually uses: paraphrase. Even the source that names Nye is saying he reworded a saying that was already the “popular accepted definition” — and it was, having run in newspapers since 1881.

artifact.linkText: The Black Hills Illustrated (1904) at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The saying has no identified author, so there is no copyright to trace: it entered print in 1881 as unsigned newspaper filler and was still being called an anonymous “old adage” in 1907. The period printings quoted here — the 1881 Detroit Free Press squib and the 1904 Black Hills Illustrated passage — are long out of copyright in the United States, but that is a fact about those particular publications, not a clearance for the modern one-line version, whose origin nobody has been able to fix.

author.name: Bill Nye (Edgar Wilson Nye)
author.kicker: The man who got the credit
author.heading: So who was Bill Nye?
author.metaLine: 1850–1896 · American humorist, lecturer & founding editor of the Laramie Boomerang
author.bio: Edgar Wilson Nye, who wrote as Bill Nye, was one of the best-known American humorists of the 1880s and 1890s — a Wyoming justice of the peace and postmaster who founded the Laramie Boomerang, then made a national name with Bill Nye’s Comic History of the United States and the lecture circuit he shared with the poet James Whitcomb Riley. He died in February 1896, aged 45. He was exactly the kind of famous frontier wit a stray mining joke would drift toward — but the one credit that names him was printed eight years after his funeral, and the historian who went looking could not find the line anywhere in Nye’s own writing.

copyAttribution: "A gold mine is a hole in the ground with a liar at the top." — not Bill Nye, and not Mark Twain. The joke first appears as unsigned newspaper filler in the Detroit Free Press, 9 November 1881. Bill Nye's name was attached in 1904, eight years after his death, by a mining book that called it his "paraphrase" and named no source; Mark Twain was first credited in 1896. Quote Investigator concludes the originator was anonymous. Source: quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Four names, none of them documented
misattribution.intro: This is a joke with an unusually crowded ownership history. Between 1892 and 1935 at least four different people were handed it in print, and the record supports none of them.

items.why: The only period source naming Nye is The Black Hills Illustrated of 1904, eight years after his death, and it describes the line as “Bill Nye’s paraphrase” of an early-day gold mine ↗ — conceding that he was reworking something already in circulation. Dan Plazak, who wrote a university-press history of mining fraud under this very title, reports that he could not find the saying in Nye’s writings ↗.

Twain’s name is attached from March 1896 onward, but Quote Investigator finds no direct evidence he used it ↗. The modern credit traces to a single second-hand sentence in The Autobiography of John Hays Hammond (1935), p. 97 — and Hammond, though he knew Twain personally, is backed by “no other authentic record that Mark Twain made this statement” ↗.

A speaker at the American Mining Congress in September 1903 handed the line to the humorist Eli Perkins — a year before Nye’s name was attached to it ↗. Plazak searched his writings too and found nothing there either ↗.

If the name calls the television presenter to mind, that is a different man entirely. The Bill Nye of the 1904 mining book was Edgar Wilson Nye (1850–1896), the frontier humorist who founded the Laramie Boomerang ↗ — and he had been dead eight years by the time the credit appeared.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke belongs to nobody. It was already circulating as unsigned newspaper filler in 1881, and Quote Investigator concludes that “the creator of the initial instance was anonymous” ↗.

context.heading: Why this joke needed an owner
lead: The 1880s and 1900s were the golden age of the American mining share — and of the American mining swindle. A promoter with a photograph of a shaft, a handful of glittering ore samples and a printing press could sell stock in a hole that had never produced an ounce. The joke about the liar at the top was not a witticism about geology; it was consumer advice, passed hand to hand by people who had learned the hard way, and it worked precisely because nobody had to have said it first.

But a good line will not stay anonymous for long. Within a decade of its first appearance the quip had been handed to a Mr. Walkup of Evanston, then to Mark Twain, then to the humorist Eli Perkins, then to Bill Nye, then to an unnamed man in Atchison, Kansas — and by 1907 a national magazine was printing the modern wording and calling it, simply, an old adage. Attribution drifts toward fame, and in the 1890s American humour had exactly three famous names to drift toward.
detailsBody: The sentence people quote today is not the sentence anyone printed. The 1881 original is three clauses long and puts the discoverer at fault. By 1892 it has compressed to “a mine is a hole in the ground and the owner is a liar.” By 1903 the owner has become a possessive — “a hole in the ground owned by a liar” — and only in January 1907 does The World’s Work print the version with the liar standing at the top.

The familiar modern one-liner welds the 1903 opening onto the 1907 ending. It reads beautifully, which is exactly why it travels — but it is a composite, and no period publication located so far contains it as a single sentence.
context.pull: “A mine is a hole in the ground. The discoverer of it is a natural liar.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located instance is the Detroit Free Press of 9 November 1881, unattributed; Mark Twain is first credited in 1896; Eli Perkins in September 1903; Bill Nye in the 1904 Black Hills Illustrated (an ascription QI calls "poorly supported"); The World's Work prints "a hole in the ground with a liar at the top" as an old adage in January 1907; and QI concludes "the creator of the initial instance was anonymous."

The 1904 book The Black Hills Illustrated, in Major A. J. Simmons's chapter "Looking Backward 56 Years," contains the sentence: "This system of financiering was worked to such a degree that Bill Nye's paraphrase of an early-day 'gold mine,' 'a hole in the ground, the owner whereof is a d—d liar,' came to be the popular accepted definition."
The Internet Archive item cu31924028873615 is the 1904 edition of The Black Hills Illustrated, George Partridge Baldwin.

twainquotes.com states the line was "attributed to Mark Twain in The Autobiography of John Hays Hammond (Farrar & Rinehart, 1935), p. 97," and that "although Hammond knew Twain personally, there is no other authentic record that Mark Twain made this statement."

Dan Plazak's miningswindles.com states there is no known documentation that Twain said or wrote it, that other sources attribute it to Bill Nye or Eli Perkins, and that "I have not been able to find the saying in the writings of either of these two."

The Wikiquote talk page for Mark Twain records the entry "A mine is a hole in the ground owned by a liar," noting it was attributed to Twain in The Autobiography of John Hays Hammond (1935), p. 97, is not recorded as actually having been said, and is also attributed to contemporaries Bill Nye and Eli Perkins.

Edgar Wilson "Bill" Nye was an American humorist born 25 August 1850 and died 22 February 1896, who founded and edited the Laramie Boomerang and wrote Bill Nye's Comic History of the United States; he lectured with James Whitcomb Riley.
